textTitles: Winter gritting: what the council does

texts.label: A
texts.title: Winter gritting: what the council does

paragraphs.text: Winter gritting: what the council does and does not do. From the first of November to the end of March, a team monitors road surface forecasts each afternoon and decides by 3 pm whether to treat the roads that night. Twelve lorries cover the priority network, which includes all A roads, bus routes, the roads to the hospital and the fire station, and the steepest hills. A full run takes about four hours, and the lorries usually go out between 6 pm and 9 pm so that the salt is down before the surface reaches freezing.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Roads that are not on the priority network are treated only when snow is forecast to lie for more than a day, and residential streets may not be treated at all in an ordinary winter. Pavements are gritted only in the town centre and at the entrances to schools. Salt spread on a dry road blows away, which is why treatment before rain is sometimes skipped even when the forecast is cold; a road that looks untreated in the morning may have been treated and washed clean overnight.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: There are two hundred yellow grit bins across the district, listed on the council website. The salt in them is for public roads and pavements, not for private drives, and taking a bag of it home is theft, however ordinary it may feel. Bins are refilled on request; report an empty one using the form on the website rather than by telephone, as the form goes directly to the depot. Residents who clear a path outside their house are not liable if someone later slips on it, provided the work was done sensibly.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The Old Dairy community fridge — how it works. The fridge stands in the porch of the community centre and is open from 8 am to 8 pm every day. Anyone may take food from it; there is no means test, no register and no limit beyond taking what you will use. Food comes from local shops, from a bakery that gives away what it has not sold, and from households with a surplus. Volunteers check and clean the fridge twice a day and record what arrives and what is taken, by weight rather than by name.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Some things cannot be accepted. Raw meat and raw fish, anything home-cooked, opened packets and anything past its use-by date must not be left in the fridge; food past its best-before date is welcome, and the difference between the two dates is explained on the notice above the door. Eggs, dairy and cooked food from a shop are accepted if they are within date and have been kept cold on the way. If you are unsure, leave the item on the shelf beside the fridge and a volunteer will decide.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The project is run by a committee of six and is funded by a small grant and by the sale of jam and chutney made from fruit that would otherwise be wasted. New volunteers are always needed for the morning check, which takes about twenty minutes; training is half an hour and no experience is required. The fridge is not a food bank and does not hold parcels, and anyone who needs regular help is given the number of the advice service, which sits in the same building on Tuesdays.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Uniform and protective equipment: what we provide and what we expect. Every employee receives three sets of uniform at the start of employment and one replacement set a year, and a further replacement is issued whenever an item is damaged at work rather than by wear. Uniform is laundered by the company for staff working with food and by the employee otherwise; where the employee launders it, a small allowance is paid with the monthly salary and does not need to be claimed.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Protective equipment is separate from uniform and is never charged to the employee. Gloves, eye protection, hearing protection and safety footwear are issued on the first day, sized individually rather than handed out in batches, and are replaced on request without explanation. An employee who is not wearing the required equipment is asked to stop work and collect it; this is not treated as a disciplinary matter unless it is repeated after a written reminder.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Personal items are allowed within limits set by safety rather than by appearance. Rings without stones, small ear studs and a watch with a smooth band may be worn in most areas but not in food preparation, where the rule is one plain band and nothing else. Long hair is tied back everywhere on the operational floor. The company does not object to visible tattoos, religious dress or covered hair, and where a safety requirement affects such an item, the supervisor arranges an alternative that meets both.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Uniform remains company property and is returned when employment ends, washed and in a bag, at the final shift or within a week. Items not returned are charged at replacement cost, which is listed in the handbook, and the charge is waived where an item was lost in circumstances the company accepts. Nothing bearing the company name may be worn outside working hours, which is a rule about responsibility rather than about the clothing itself: what a person does in uniform is read as what the company does.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Handling complaints by telephone. The first thirty seconds decide most calls. Give your name, let the customer describe the problem without interruption, and write down what they say rather than what you assume they mean; people who feel interrupted repeat themselves for longer, so listening is faster than it looks. Do not apologise for the company before you know what happened, and do not defend the company either; say that you will find out.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Establish the facts in a fixed order: what was bought, when, what has happened since, and what the customer wants. The last of these is asked directly and is frequently smaller than expected — an apology, a replacement part, a delivery date that is actually true. Where the request is within your authority, agree it on the call and say when it will happen; where it is not, say who will decide, by when, and how the customer will be told. Never end a call with an open ending.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Records matter more than memory. Every call is logged the same day with the customer’s words in quotation marks where they matter, the action agreed, and the deadline; a colleague picking up the case must be able to continue it without ringing the customer back for information they have already given. Repeating the same questions is the single most common cause of a complaint becoming a second complaint, and it is entirely within our control.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Some calls are different. A customer who is abusive is warned once, politely and clearly, and the call is ended if the behaviour continues; the log records the words used, and no member of staff is expected to remain on such a call. A complaint that concerns safety is escalated the same hour rather than the same day, whatever else is in the queue. And a customer who has been let down twice goes to the duty manager automatically, because a third failure is worth more to avoid than an hour of anyone’s time.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Handwriting was expected to disappear twice: once when the typewriter arrived and again when every child was given a keyboard. It has not, and the reasons are more interesting than the prediction. Adults write less than their grandparents did and in shorter forms — a list, a card, a note on a form — but they write, and schools that removed handwriting from the curriculum have quietly put parts of it back, usually after finding that something else went with it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The something else is the part that surprised people. Studies comparing students who took notes by hand with students who typed them have found repeatedly that the typists produce more words and remember less, especially when tested on understanding rather than on recall of facts. The explanation offered is that typing is fast enough to allow transcription while handwriting is not, so the writer has to decide what matters, and the deciding is the learning. The effect is modest, has been replicated unevenly, and points in one direction.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Learning to form letters appears to matter for reading as well. Children who practise writing letters by hand recognise those letters faster afterwards than children who have practised only by selecting them on a screen, and brain imaging finds different patterns of activity in the two groups. The proposed mechanism is not mysterious: making a shape repeatedly, with variation and with errors, builds a more flexible idea of what the shape is than selecting a perfect version does.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Against this, the case for keyboards is strong and is often stated badly. A child whose handwriting is slow or painful writes shorter and worse sentences than the same child dictating or typing, and for children with certain motor or coordination difficulties the keyboard is the difference between writing and not writing. Insisting on handwriting for everyone is therefore not a neutral policy, and the sensible schools hold both: teach the hand, and remove it as a barrier for the children for whom it is one.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Joined writing is the part of the argument that has least evidence behind it. It was introduced because it was faster with a nib that caught on the paper when lifted, and the nib has gone; studies comparing joined and printed styles find little difference in speed or legibility once children are fluent, and the fastest adult writers use a mixture. Several school systems have therefore dropped the requirement to join, kept the requirement to write legibly and at a reasonable speed, and reported no loss.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Speed has a threshold rather than a scale. A student who writes below a certain number of letters a minute cannot take notes, answer an examination question at length or draft an essay without losing the thread, and that threshold is where most handwriting difficulties actually bite. Above it, further speed adds little. This is a useful way to set a target, because it replaces an aesthetic judgement about neatness with a measurable one about whether the hand keeps up with the thought.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Signatures and law are a smaller argument than they were. Electronic signatures are now accepted for most purposes in most countries, and the handwritten signature survives mainly where it is a ritual with witnesses: a will, a marriage, a deed. Banks stopped comparing signatures to cards long ago. What remains is a residue of documents that require the hand, and a much larger residue of situations in which people sign because signing marks the moment as serious, which is a social function rather than a legal one.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The likely future is the one that is already here: handwriting as a specialised skill used for a narrow set of tasks, taught because those tasks matter and because learning it appears to help with something else, and no longer taught as a general measure of education. That is a demotion rather than a disappearance, and it puts handwriting roughly where mental arithmetic sits — still worth having, no longer a reason to fail a child, and quietly useful in ways that are hard to argue for in a curriculum meeting.
paragraphs.label: H
